source_text: CAPUT NONUM, Resurrectionem mortuorum possibilem esse, principiis naturalibus probatur. Haec de iis qui resurrectionem carnis perperam negaverunt: sequuntur meliores, qui recte firmiterque asserunt, eam 1. esse possibilem, 2. certo futuram, 3. ejus causas, 4. modum, 5. necessarium consequens.
english: CHAPTER NINE. The resurrection of the dead is proved to be possible from natural principles.

These things concerning those who wrongly denied the resurrection of the flesh: there follow the better ones, who rightly and firmly assert (1) that it is possible, (2) that it is certainly future, (3) its causes, (4) its mode, (5) its necessary consequence.

source_text: Ad rem vero, de quo Gregorius Nyssenus, qui de resurrectione Christi tres doctissimas scripsit orationes, libro quem Structurae veteres dixerunt, de structura hominis cap. 25. 26. & 27. docet, animam affectione & amore a natura singulari corpus, in cujus quasi contubernio fuit, prosequi, & ineffabili naturae tractu ad ejus conjunctionem ferri; idque hoc exemplo declarat vivum argentum. Artis vero typi sunt varii. Primus est figulinae artis, quo utitur Gregorius Nyssenus orat. 3. de resurrectione. Sicut enim figulus vas e luto fingit & ad solem exsiccat, forte autem confractum & redactum in lutum refingit restituitque: ita & Deus corpora nostra. Secundus est Achilles aureus qui prius fuerat aeneus. Tertius est artis vitriariae: nam ex arena & nitro perspicuum vitrum efficitur, sunt etiam vitra e cineribus. Quartus denique est artis chymicae: e cineribus urticarum paratum lixivium si frigori exponatur, in glacie illa urticae conspiciendae sese praebent. Hactenus vidimus resurrectionem carnis esse possibilem.
english: But to the thing: concerning which Gregory of Nyssa, who wrote three most learned orations on Christ's resurrection, in the book which the ancients called On Structure, On the Making of Man chapters 25, 26, and 27, teaches that the soul by affection and love from a singular nature pursues the body in whose quasi-companionship it was, and by an ineffable pull of nature is carried to its conjunction; and he declares that by the example of quicksilver.

But the types of art are various. The first is of the potter's art, which Gregory of Nyssa uses in his third oration On the Resurrection. For just as the potter forms a vessel from clay and dries it in the sun, but if by chance it is broken and reduced to clay he reshapes and restores it: so also God our bodies. The second is the golden Achilles who formerly had been bronze. The third is of the glassmaker's art: for from sand and nitre transparent glass is made, and there are also glasses from ashes. The fourth finally is of chemical art: if a lye prepared from the ashes of nettles is exposed to cold, in that ice the nettles offer themselves to be seen. Hitherto we have seen that the resurrection of the flesh is possible.

source_text: Idcirco gentiles respondere possunt, desiderium ad unionem si quod animae insit, unione ea quam semel obtinuit satis expleri, neque animam a corpore perfectionem quandam accipere, sed corpori potius communicare: quin per separationem ad summum rerum gradum propius jam accessisse, atque adeo intelligentiis & Deo similiorem esse. III. A divina justitia. Tertio, inquit Thomas, ex divina providentia peccantibus poena debetur, & bene agentibus praemium. In hac autem vita homines ex anima & corpore compositi peccant. Debetur igitur homini & secundum animam & secundum corpus praemium vel poena. Verum haec ratio in hoc genere omnium validissima est, quam prisci doctores passim & vehementer urgent, maxime Tertullianus.
english: Therefore the Gentiles can reply that if any desire toward union is in the soul, it is sufficiently filled by that union which it once obtained, and that the soul does not receive some perfection from the body but rather communicates to the body: nay that by separation it has already approached nearer the highest grade of things, and so is more like the intelligences and God.

III. From divine justice. Third, Thomas says, from divine providence punishment is owed to those sinning, and reward to those acting well. But in this life humans composed of soul and body sin. Therefore reward or punishment is owed to the human both according to soul and according to body. And truly this reason is the strongest of all in this kind, which the ancient doctors everywhere and vehemently urge, especially Tertullian.

source_text: IV. A principio ab omnibus concesso, nempe, ut actiones sunt suppositorum, ita & passiones, adeoque & praemia & poenae: jam vero certum est, solam animam hominem non esse. Verum si fatendum est quod res est, haec ratio suadet, non tamen cogit & evincit. Cum enim anima sit princeps actionis causa, corpus vero instrumentum, probari nequit justitiam sibi non constare, si princeps causa praemio vel poena afficiatur, relicto interim instrumento; praesertim si res eo devenerit.
english: IV. From a principle conceded by all — namely, as actions are of the subjects, so also passions, and so also rewards and punishments: but now it is certain that the soul alone is not the human. Yet if what is the case must be confessed, this reason persuades, yet does not compel and prove. For since the soul is the principal cause of action, but the body the instrument, it cannot be proved that justice does not stand consistent with itself if the principal cause is affected with reward or punishment, the instrument meanwhile left aside — especially if the matter has come to that.

source_text: II. A naturali hominis desiderio, quo ad felicitatem tendit. Deinde, ait Thomas, ostensum est naturale hominis desiderium ad felicitatem tendere. Felicitas autem ultima est felicis perfectio. Cuicunque igitur deest aliquid ad perfectionem, nondum habet perfectam felicitatem, quia nondum ejus desiderium totaliter quietatur. Omne enim imperfectum perfectionem consequi naturaliter appetit. Anima autem a corpore separata desiderium naturale ad unionem cum corpore retinet; ergo nondum perfecte beata est absque corpore.
english: II. From the human's natural desire by which he tends toward felicity. Next, Thomas says, it has been shown that the human's natural desire tends toward felicity. But last felicity is the perfection of the happy one. Therefore to whomsoever something is lacking toward perfection, he does not yet have perfect felicity, because his desire is not yet totally quieted. For every imperfect thing naturally appetites to obtain perfection. But the soul separated from the body retains a natural desire toward union with the body; therefore it is not yet perfectly blessed without the body.

source_text: RATIO I. Est a naturali desiderio & inclinatione. Anima enim corpori naturaliter unitur. Est enim secundum suam essentiam corporis forma. Est igitur contra naturam animae, absque corpore esse. Nihil autem quod est contra naturam, potest esse perpetuum. Non igitur perpetuo erit anima absque corpore. Cum igitur perpetuo maneat, oportet eam iterato corpori conjungi, quod est resurgere. Immortalitas igitur animarum exigere videtur resurrectionem corporum futuram.
english: REASON I. It is from natural desire and inclination. For the soul is naturally united to the body. For according to its essence it is the form of the body. Therefore it is against the soul's nature to be without a body. But nothing that is against nature can be perpetual. Therefore the soul will not perpetually be without a body. Since therefore it remains perpetually, it must be joined again to the body, which is to rise. Therefore the immortality of souls seems to demand that the resurrection of bodies will be future.

source_text: Ad hominem pro resurrectione carnis argumentantur patres, dum contra Ethnicos ex exemplorum historiis vel potius fabulis eam asserunt. Sic Theophilus Antiochenus lib. 1. ad Autolycum: Credis, inquit, Herculem, quem flamma absumpsit, vivere; & Aesculapium fulmine tactum vitae restitutum: qua dementia est, nolle dare fidem illis quae Deus loquitur? Sic Aeneas Gazeus philosophus Platonicus Christianus, florens quinto post Christum saeculo sub Imperatoribus Zenone & Anastasio, in Dialogo de immortalitate animae & corporum resurrectione, quem inscripsit Theophrastum, sub persona Theophrasti: An, inquit, terrenum hoc corpus resuscitandum iri putas? At id miraculi simile fuerit, quandoquidem diffluxit & dispersum est. Et aliud quidem a piscibus limatum, aliud ab avibus discerptum est; eaque animalia vicissim ab aliis capta & absumpta sunt, ut ne ullum quidem vestigium humani corporis supersit. Et respondet sub persona Axithei. Plinius quoque nonnullos recenset qui elati revixerint, lib. 7. naturalis historiae cap. 52. Haec sunt argumenta ad hominem, quae neminem alium premunt quam eum qui talia credit.
english: To the person the fathers argue for the resurrection of the flesh when against the pagans they assert it from histories of examples, or rather from fables. So Theophilus of Antioch (To Autolycus book 1): You believe, he says, that Hercules, whom the flame consumed, lives; and that Aesculapius struck by lightning was restored to life: what madness is it to refuse to give faith to those things which God speaks?

So Aeneas of Gaza, a Platonic Christian philosopher flourishing in the fifth century after Christ under the emperors Zeno and Anastasius, in his Dialogue on the Immortality of the Soul and the Resurrection of Bodies, which he titled Theophrastus, under Theophrastus's person: Do you think, he says, that this earthly body is to be resuscitated? But that would be like a miracle, seeing that it has flowed apart and been dispersed. And one part indeed has been filed by fishes, another torn by birds; and those animals in turn have been caught and consumed by others, so that not even any vestige of the human body remains. And he answers under Axitheus's person. Pliny also recounts some who revived after being carried out (Natural History book 7, chapter 52). These are arguments to the person, which press no one other than him who believes such things.

source_text: II. Etsi enim carnis resurrectionem futuram esse, lumine naturae demonstrari non possit: tamen eam possibilem & consentaneam esse probari potest. Hunc aphorismum defendunt Theologi in scholis. Johannes Scotus non male libro 4. sententiarum distin. 43. quaest. 2. Nec a priori, inquit, per rationem principii intrinseci in homine, nec a posteriori per rationem alicujus operationis vel perfectionis congruentis homini, potest probari necessario resurrectio innitendo lumini naturae. Ergo hoc tanquam omnino certum non tenetur, nisi per fidem. Et postea: Ex his apparet, quanta sit gratia & liberalitas cordis creatoris, qui nos per fidem certissimos reddidit in his quae pertinent ad finem nostrum & perpetuitatem sempiternam. Adducit in hunc sensum illud Augustini lib. 13. de Trinit. cap. 9. Humanis argumentationibus haec invenire conantes, vix pauci magno praediti ingenio, abundantes otio, doctrinisque subtilissimis eruditi, ad indagandam solius animae immortalitatem pervenire potuerunt. Fides autem ista totum hominem immortalem futurum, qui utique constat ex anima & corpore, & ob hoc vere beatum, non argumentatione humana, sed divina authoritate promittit.
english: II. For although that the resurrection of the flesh will be future cannot be demonstrated by the light of nature: yet that it is possible and fitting can be proved. Theologians in the schools defend this aphorism. John Scotus not badly in Sentences book 4, distinction 43, question 2: Neither a priori, he says, by reason of an intrinsic principle in the human, nor a posteriori by reason of some operation or perfection congruent to the human, can resurrection be proved as necessary by leaning on the light of nature. Therefore this is not held as altogether certain except by faith. And afterward: From these things it appears how great is the grace and liberality of the Creator's heart, who through faith has made us most certain in those things which pertain to our end and everlasting perpetuity.

He brings to this sense that of Augustine (On the Trinity book 13, chapter 9): Those attempting to find these things by human argumentations — scarcely a few endowed with great genius, abounding in leisure, and trained in the most subtle doctrines — have been able to arrive at investigating the immortality of the soul alone. But that faith promises that the whole human will be immortal, who certainly consists of soul and body, and on that account truly blessed, not by human argumentation but by divine authority.

source_text: Sunt autem aphorismi hujus duo membra, unum quo resurrectionem necessario futuram e lumine naturae demonstrari posse negatur: alterum quo eam possibilem & vero consentaneam esse, ex eo probari posse affirmatur. Prioris ratio est, quia tum resuscitatio, tum glorificatio pendet a libera Dei voluntate, quae aliunde sciri aut demonstrari nequit nisi e revelatione, quae ab ipso libere itidem & benigne facta nobis pandit tantum mysterium spectans ad beatitudinem & ultimum finem nostrum. Posterioris vero rationes afferuntur vel ad hominem, vel ad rem.
english: But of this aphorism there are two members: one by which it is denied that the resurrection can be demonstrated as necessarily future from the light of nature; the other by which it is affirmed that it can be proved from that light to be possible and truly fitting. The reason of the former is that both resuscitation and glorification hang on God's free will, which cannot otherwise be known or demonstrated except from revelation, which, made by him likewise freely and kindly, opens to us so great a mystery looking toward beatitude and our last end. But the reasons of the latter are brought either to the person or to the thing.
